messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stack_alloc_speed
parts: Thanks for diving into this. More inline.

On Mar 3, 2014, at 10:33 PM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:

>
> With develop, I get a std::bad_alloc exception for the stack_alloc_speed test with clang++-3.5 (shown below) and all versions of g++
>
> ==1550==ERROR: MemorySanitizer failed to allocate 0x1fffffffffff (35184372088831) bytes at address 35184372088832 (12)

That's whack. No idea why it's trying to allocate so many bytes here.
The error makes it look like it's trying to swap:
> FATAL: MemorySanitizer can not mmap the shadow memory.
Any idea what PIE or -pie are?

> FATAL: Make sure to compile with -fPIE and to link with -pie.
> FATAL: Disabling ASLR is known to cause this error.

ASLR? That looks like "address space layout randomization". Does
that mean the test is just jumping up where it tries to do the allocation
each time? That doesn't seem realistic, but would cause the fail.
> FATAL: If running under GDB, try 'set disable-randomization off'.

Is that supposed to un-disable ASLR? Too many negations!

But it is jumped way up in memory:

>
> 0xffffffffff600000-0xffffffffff601000 [vsyscall]
> ==1550==End of process memory map.
> make: *** [test/unit/memory/stack_alloc_speed] Error 77
>
>
> The gdb output is not any more helpful
Thanks for trying!

>
> It passes if I change the second loop to terminate at 10000
>
> goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ cat src/test/unit/memory/stack_alloc_speed_test.cpp
> #include <stan/memory/stack_alloc.hpp>
> #include <gtest/gtest.h>
>
> TEST(stack_alloc, speed_of_allocator) {
> stan::memory::stack_alloc allocator;
> for (size_t m = 0; m < 10000; m++) {
> for (size_t n = 1; n <= 100000; ++n) {
> allocator.alloc(n);
> }
> allocator.recover_all();
> }
> }

I think that's more illuminating because chaning that to 10K, it's 10K * 10K, so
it should just use 100MB. Whereas with 100K * 10K, it's using 1GB. Still, I
wouldn't think that'd balk.

I don't see why recover_all doesn't reset back to the beginning. Here's
the code:

inline void recover_all() {
cur_block_ = 0;
next_loc_ = blocks_[0];
cur_block_end_ = next_loc_ + sizes_[0];
}

These ever-shifting C++ compilers are really frustrating. I take it you
did this in earlier compilers without a problem?

Here's the sanitizer code that's throwing the error:

https://llvm.org/svn/llvm-project/compiler-rt/trunk/lib/msan/msan_allocator.cc

But I'm not going to worry about it if only the sanitizer is causing
problems. From looking at the code, it looks like it never deallocs (see
MSanDeallocate function). It's own doc:

http://clang.llvm.org/docs/MemorySanitizer.html

says it's an experimental tool.

Also, we don't want to check that all of our allocated memory is
clean --- we intentionally allocate memory that we don't ever fill
because we have sizes that overrun boundaries of blocks so have to
go in the next block. Could this be the source of the problem?

- Bob

This is helpful.  

The test's failing when it tries to allocate a 2GB block.

Ah, I figured it out. Not a bug.

I couple days ago I configured that tab to limit the memory of a process to 2GB when I was trying to investigate that memory leak that I emailed you about. Then I forgot I was using that same tab when I was trying to do the unit tests.

That said, we need to keep all individual tests below 2GB (at least with clang++) because the most basic tier of availability on the Columbia cluster is limited to 2GB per process. There are hundreds of cores available for that purpose and we can basically do 1 core per unit test. If you need more memory, you have to wait for one of the much fewer number of big memory slots to become available.

Ben
